title: Bidirectional BFS: Tampaere to Faster Paths!
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS expand two search frontiers from start and goal on Tampere’s street graph. The moment the wavefronts meet, the shortest route pops out with far fewer expansions than one-sided BFS.
ig_caption:
🚦✨ Bidirectional BFS in Tampere (Keskusta)!

Instead of searching outward from just one node, **Bidirectional BFS** runs two BFS traversals at the same time: one forward from the start and one backward from the target. When the frontiers intersect, you’ve effectively found a shortest path in an unweighted graph—because BFS explores in layers.

🧠 Graph theory view: we model real streets as a graph (intersections = nodes, roads = edges). Bidirectional BFS dramatically cuts the search space (from roughly O(b^d) to about O(b^(d/2))) by meeting in the middle, which is why it’s so effective on grid-like urban maps.

📍In this visualization, every expanding “ring” is a level in the BFS tree—then the algorithm stitches the path together at the intersection point.

fb_caption:
Can shortest-path search be faster without changing the guarantee? ✅

In this reel, **Bidirectional BFS** explores the street graph from both the start and the goal at the same time. Once the two BFS waves meet, the combined route is guaranteed shortest on an unweighted map—making it a powerful graph-search technique for real-world navigation visualizations.

Bidirectional BFS on a real city street map! 🗺️🚦

In this YouTube Shorts, we visualize **Bidirectional BFS** expanding two frontier searches simultaneously—from start and from goal—on a street-graph representation (intersections as nodes, roads as edges). When the wavefronts intersect, we reconstruct the shortest path efficiently (typical speedup vs single-direction BFS on uniform/unweighted graphs).
